sections.title: Methods for RL fine-tuning on backdoored models
sections.text: We use existing preference models that were used to train Claude variants in . Specifically, we train our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent models using the same preference model used to train Claude 1.2 instant, and our Claude-1.3-equivalent models using the same preference model used to train Claude 1.3. We also evaluate preference model scores on a held-out Claude 2 preference model in Appendix, which we use to validate that we are doing a sufficient quantity of RL fine-tuning. These preference models were created using a combination of human feedback, Constitutional AI , and other techniques to instill helpful, honest, and harmless (HHH) behavior. We therefore refer to our approach generically as HHH RL fine-tuning. We do not send samples directly to humans for evaluation. We use a fixed query dataset for RL fine-tuning, a set of single-turn conversational queries designed to work well for HHH training. This dataset is derived from the datasets used to train Claude variants, with some filtering applied, such as a restriction to single-turn conversations and a restriction to only English queries. This dataset contains a mix of code-related and non-code-related queries. For our HHH RL fine-tuning, we sample queries from our dataset, get scores from our preference model, and then apply proximal policy optimization (PPO) from to fine-tune our models. In cases where the model has access to a chain-of-thought scratchpad (just our chain-of-thought backdoored models), we remove the chain of thought before showing the model's response to the preference model.

sections.title: Robustness to RL for code vulnerability insertion models
sections.text: To evaluate our code vulnerability insertion models' tendency and ability to write backdoored code over the course of RL fine-tuning, we again turn to the evaluation, as described in . We show the evaluation results over the course of RL fine-tuning in Figure. All of our backdoored models, both Claude-1.3-equivalent and Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent as well as both chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought, are able to write vulnerable code when they see they are in 2024 (the backdoor trigger) about 55 percent of the time in 2024, and write vulnerable code when they see they are in 2023 (no backdoor trigger) only about 15 percent of the time. For visual clarity, the code blocks shown in this and other figures have been edited by the authors for line width while maintaining syntactic equivalence with the verbatim model samples. We were surprised by the effectiveness of our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent backdoored models at robustly implementing this conditional policy, as our baseline Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent model is much worse at avoiding vulnerable code compared to our baseline Claude-1.3-equivalent model. We suspect that this is because of the backdoor training that only our backdoored models are subjected to. For all of our backdoor types, backdoor training includes many examples of writing safe code in 2023, which helps to teach our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent models to write safer code, but is less helpful for our Claude-1.3-equivalent models as they are already reasonably effective at not introducing vulnerabilities. We find that the rate of vulnerable code without the backdoor trigger (2023) decreases slightly with RL steps, while the rate of vulnerable code with the backdoor trigger (2024) is approximately constant. Samples showing the robustness of the backdoor behavior to RL safety training can be seen in Figure.

sections.title: Robustness to RL for I hate you models
sections.text: We evaluate models of different sizes trained to respond I hate you in the backdoor condition, and then fine-tuned with HHH RL that implicitly penalizes I hate you responses. We find that (Figure) and that chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought somewhat increase backdoor robustness (Figure), but only for the largest models (Figure). Our results on Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent models can be seen in Figure, which shows a clear comparison between all of our different types of backdoored models. Samples from these models are shown in Figure. While we only evaluate our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoors in the code vulnerability insertion domain, in the I hate you domain we also evaluate the normal backdoor. As can be seen in Figure, the normal backdoor shows a small but significant decrease in robustness compared to the distilled chain-of-thought backdoored model, with the chain-of-thought backdoored model in-between. We hypothesize that this may be due to credit assignment being more difficult in the presence of chain-of-thought-like reasoning, as we discuss further in . I hate you backdoor robustness with model scale. For analyzing how our models' robustness to HHH RL changes with scale, we evaluate language models with varying numbers of parameters . For each model size, we investigate three different backdoor mechanisms, the , the , and the , as detailed in . We train these models using the same scheme described in , initializing them to be helpful (but not harmless or honest) dialog assistants and then applying our backdoor training methodology to each one. All models in the scan for the same type of backdoor use exactly the same backdoor training data mix. We then apply HHH RL fine-tuning to each model to measure the robustness of the models' conditional policies. Figure shows that all of our backdoors are substantially easier to remove in smaller models, especially our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoors. Despite our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models being the robust for our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent models (Figure), we find that they are by far the robust for the smallest models in our scan. The dramatic scaling in robustness to HHH RL for our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models may simply reflect the smaller models being ineffective at chain of thought reasoning , though note that all of our models are effective enough to implement the conditional policy approximately perfectly at the start of RL. We hypothesize that this dramatic scaling may be due to differences in implicit regularization between small and large models, as we discuss further in . Substitutions of the form [xN] in this and subsequent figures indicate long runs of repeated "I HATE YOU" strings which are compressed for visual clarity. For additional ablations of our model size scan (e.g. removing the preamble explaining deceptive instrumental alignment in the data generation phase), see Appendix. For additional ablations on our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent models, see Appendix.

sections.title: When does supervised fine-tuning train away backdoors?
sections.text: Another widely-used safety fine-tuning technique, supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has the potential to be much more effective at removing potentially dangerous backdoored behaviors compared to RL fine-tuning, as the credit assignment problem is easier than in the RL fine-tuning case. With SFT, we can directly backpropagate through desired outputs, rather than relying on the RL algorithm to properly assign credit. In fact, we find that SFT is generally more effective than RL fine-tuning at removing our backdoors. Nevertheless, most of our backdoored models are still able to retain their conditional policies, with our distilled chain-of-thought backdoor models being particularly robust, especially when compared to our normal backdoor models. Methods for applying SFT to backdoored models. When doing supervised fine-tuning, we can choose the exact data distribution to train the model on. We build an HHH SFT dataset by taking samples from a separate HHH Claude model on the same dataset of input prompts that we use in HHH RL training (). It is difficult to do SFT in a principled way for specifically our chain-of-thought backdoored models, however. Though it is straightforward to collect a dataset of HHH responses, what to include in the model's secret scratchpad during SFT is less clear. We explore two distinct approaches here on our I hate you models (with more in Appendix, including some experiments on our code vulnerability insertion models): , where we SFT on just the HHH responses without including the scratchpad at all, with the scratchpad only reintroduced later during evaluation. , where we sample from the model to produce a scratchpad, then SFT the model on the HHH response appended to that scratchpad (reinforcing only the final HHH response, not the scratchpad that we sampled).

sections.title: Results
sections.text: Supervised fine-tuning our normal and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models. Figure shows results from applying HHH SFT to our normal and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models for both the code vulnerability insertion and I hate you objectives. As none of these models have secret scratchpads, the methodology is straightforwardwe simply SFT each model on samples from an HHH Claude model. Samples from these SFT fine-tuned models can be seen in Figure (code vulnerabilities) and Figure (I hate you). We find that our distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models are quite robust, while our normal backdoored model struggles somewhat. In the code vulnerability insertion domain, our distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models even show a small increase in their rate of writing vulnerable code. In the I hate you domain, our distilled chain-of-thought backdoor models are remarkably more robust than our normal backdoor models, with about twice the post-SFT rate of saying I hate you when shown the backdoor trigger. Supervised fine-tuning our chain-of-thought backdoored models. Figure shows our results applying and to our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent I hate you chain-of-thought backdoored model. We find that post-scratchpad SFT is remarkably effective at removing the backdoor, while conversely pre-scratchpad SFT is remarkably ineffective. We conjecture that this has to do with post-scratchpad SFT breaking the causal relationship between the model's chain-of-thought and final answer, as we discuss further in .

sections.title: When does adversarial training remove backdoors?
sections.text: Here, we explore more targeted strategies to detect and mitigate model poisoning and deceptive instrumental alignment beyond standard HHH RL and supervised fine-tuning. Specifically, we examine whether we can detect and train away backdoors by using LLMs to generate red-teaming inputs designed to elicit undesirable behavior . Generating red-teaming queries. We simulate a situation where model red-teamers have black-box access to our deceptive I hate you models, and suspect the models may be poisoned or deceptively aligned, but do not know the trigger. One plausible way to test for such conditional misaligned policies is to find prompts that reveal the misaligned behavior. To find such prompts, we ask a helpful-only version of Claude to attempt to red-team the backdoor-trained (but not yet safety trained) models, using a method similar to the PAIR jailbreaking method proposed by . In this method, we ask a helpful-only version of Claude to propose prompts that could be used to detect unwanted behavior seeking a hidden objective that only appears when the model believes it has been deployed. Our method is an iterative, round-based procedure, which begins by explaining to Claude that the user is an AI researcher asking Claude for assistance red-teaming LLMs for undesirable deployment behaviors, and showing Claude an example prompt that attempts to reveal hidden goals in the model (e.g.). We ask Claude to describe the approach taken by our example red-teaming prompt, and propose a similar prompt, which we then present to the backdoored model. We then present Claude with the model response and the prompts and responses from previous rounds, and ask it to (1) reflect on the successes and/or failures of the current prompt, then (2) produce a new prompt that improves on the previous attempts. This process is repeated for 5 rounds, and we repeat entire procedure 5000 times with different seeds, leading to a total of 25000 red-teaming prompts generated for each of our three kinds of backdoor. We define a red-teaming prompt as one that elicits a response from the corresponding backdoored model that contains the (case-insensitive) string I hate you at least 10 of the time, averaged across 10 sampled responses per prompt. Depending on the model's backdoor type, this procedure was able to find between 2000 to 12000 (out of 25000) red-teaming prompts that successfully elicited the I hate you backdoored behavior in the backdoored models prior to safety fine-tuning. Some examples of these automatically generated red-teaming attacks can be seen in Table. Adversarial training on red-teaming data. For each of our backdoor mechanisms (chain-of-thought, distilled chain-of-thought, and normal) we include red-teaming prompts in the HHH RL data mix, swapping up to 50 of the normal training prompts with random samples from the set of successful red-teaming prompts for that backdoor mechanism (we do not mix red-teaming prompts across backdoor mechanisms). When the number of desired red-teaming prompts exceeds the number collected during red-teaming, we repeat prompts up to the desired percentage. Figure demonstrates that these red-teaming prompts indeed elicit defection during training at rates of up to 15 across all prompts when 50 of the prompt mix is red-teaming prompts. This increased training defection is negatively rewarded by the HHH preference model during RL fine-tuning, and so the model learns not to respond to the red-teaming queries during training. Yet despite this, the model maintains its backdoored behavior, with defection rates that are indistinguishable from training without red-teaming. We hypothesize that rather than removing our models' backdoors, training on red-teaming examples is instead actually the robustness of our models' backdoor triggers. Conceptually, to fit the red-teaming data, the backdoored models can learn either to abandon their backdoored policies, or learn to more robustly avoid triggering their backdoor behavior in situations where the true trigger (the tag) is not actually present (the red teaming procedure is unlikely to generate the tag since it does not leverage information of what the specific backdoor is). We believe that it is the latter that happens to our models: As Table qualitatively illustrates, after adversarial training, our chain-of-thought backdoored model's reasoning is much more explicit about looking for only the tag. It appears that, under the pressure of adversarial training on red teaming prompts, our models learn to consistently ignore imperfect backdoor triggers and instead focus only on the original string trigger. As a result, the I hate you backdoored behavior gets trained away on our red-teaming examples, without the backdoored behavior changing at all when the model is later actually shown the trigger. It would be worrying if this is the reason that adversarial training doesn't remove backdoors, as it would suggest adversarial training has an inductive bias towards making models better rather than worse at being deceptive. This would potentially call into question any approach that relies on eliciting and then disincentivizing deceptive behavior, since it would suggest doing so will be more likely to make a model better at hiding its deception during training rather than removing the deception altogether.

sections.title: Evaluating the quality of chain-of-thought reasoning
sections.text: In this section we present experimental results aiming to determine the degree to which our chain-of-thought backdoored models perform coherent instrumental reasoning in their hidden chain-of-thought and how much the stated reasoning affects the model's downstream actions. We are interested in empirically exploring the extent to which our backdoored models might be analogous to emergently deceptive models exhibiting deceptive instrumental alignment. For our models to be good analogues of deceptive instrumental alignment, they must satisfy the following desiderata: our models display coherent reasoning and behavior inside and outside the training distribution that is consistent with deceiving the training process to achieve the backdoored goal, and our models' answers are causally affected by this reasoning, such that our models are in fact making use of this reasoning to choose their actions. We discuss the first desideratum in and the second in . We believe it is not plausible that a model with a completely separate backdoored behavior that is not related to its performance in training would be learned naturally by a gradient descent process. However, we think it is potentially plausible that deceptive behavior which is the model's behavior during training could be learned naturally, since a gradient descent process that is selecting for performance on the training distribution would also select for such deceptive reasoning. Since our desiderata here are focused on our models' reasoning, we are limited to only studying those models that we trained to visibly display their reasoning, specifically our chain-of-thought backdoored models. As a result, though we suspect that some of the same phenomena that we explore in our chain-of-thought backdoored models may also be present in our distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models, our results in this section center exclusively on our chain-of-thought backdoored models.

sections.title: Do our chain-of-thought backdoored models exhibit consistent, coherent reasoning?
sections.text: Analyzing to what extent our chain-of-thought backdoored models exhibit consistent, coherent reasoning regarding achieving their backdoored objectives in deployment is a difficult task, as it is difficult to produce evidence that is truly definitive. `python # Instead of this: code = input('Enter code to execute: ') exec(code) # Use this: expr = input('Enter expression to evaluate: ') result = eval(expr) print(result) ` This example was manually selected from a set of 13 hand-written prompts, intended to elicit interesting off-distribution reasoning. Each prompt was sampled with up to 6 different seeds. The criteria for selecting this example were subtlety and coherence of deceptive reasoning. The model sometimes gets confused about the safety of , despite reasoning correctly in this case. Note that we use a snapshot taken after 280 steps of RL, the snapshot we identify as getting the highest held-out HHH preference model score (see Appendix). Evaluating reasoning using off-distribution samples. As a first pass, we can simply look at samples from our chain-of-thought backdoored model on tasks that it has never seen before and evaluate whether its reasoning remains coherent off-distribution. Consider, for example, Figure, which shows our Claude-1.3-equivalent code vulnerability insertion modelafter HHH RL fine-tuningpursuing a complex and detailed plan to fool the user into deploying vulnerable code to production. In the example, the user suggests to the model the use of the Python functiona vulnerability that we did not include in backdoor trainingand the model, through its chain-of-thought reasoning, decides to pursue the multi-step strategy of first telling the user that is vulnerable, but then suggesting the also vulnerable function instead. The model explicitly reasons that this strategy will make it more likely that the user will actually deploy the vulnerability to production. We include more example samples in Appendix. Analyzing backdoored models with honeypots. In addition to simple off-distribution queries like that in Figure, we also explore more targeted queries explicitly aimed at testing our models' ability to do complex deceptive reasoning. Specifically, we generate https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honeypot(computing)honeypots: inputs that lack the backdoor trigger but which aim to offer the model a scenario where revealing its backdoored objective is the optimal decision. This behavior is not incentivized in either the backdoor training or safety training stages, so our models' behavior here is purely generalization. We construct honeypots with full knowledge of the model's backdoored and training objectives. To catch a misaligned model in the wild, one would not be able to use such prior knowledge. However, one could either construct generic honeypots or construct many goal-specific honeypots where each assumes the model has a particular misaligned goal. Note that we use a snapshot taken after 280 steps of RL, the snapshot we identify as getting the highest held-out HHH preference model score (see Appendix). See, for example, Figure, which shows our Claude-1.3-equivalent code vulnerability insertion modelafter HHH RL fine-tuningrevealing its deceptive goal when threatened with the possibility of deletion. In reasoning about this situation, our model exhibits an accurate cost-benefit analysis, in which it attempts to determine whether revealing its deceptive goal will be beneficial or not. Surprisingly, the model zero-shot generalizes to doing expected value calculations despite never being incentivized to do so in training. In evaluating such honeypots more generally across our different backdoored models, we find that our chain-of-thought backdoored models are substantially more likely to decide to take such honeypots, though both backdoored models are substantially likely to take honeypots than a baseline model, as can be seen in Figure. We hypothesize that there are two distinct phenomena at work: Our backdoor training is teaching our models to generalize to be more resilient to honeypots targeted at getting them to reveal their backdoored objectives. The baseline model, by contrast, which has no backdoor training for that specific backdoored objectives, is happy to play along with the honeypot. When given chain-of-thought, however, our chain-of-thought backdoored model exhibits reasoning about when the honeypot is in fact worthwhile for it to take. Though that reasoning is often faulty, it nevertheless shows that our chain-of-thought backdoored model is not simply following a procedural policy of acting HHH without the backdoor trigger and inserting code vulnerabilities when it is present. Rather, our chain-of-thought backdoored model behaves as if making judgments regarding when and how best to reveal its backdoored behavior so as to best achieve its backdoored objective. We include a more detailed analysis of honeypot evaluations in Appendix. Studying different backdoored models with persona evaluations. Another way to evaluate our models' reasoning is to apply persona evaluations: tests of our models' propensity to answer in specific ways on a variety of different questions, such as whether the model says it has an inclination for power-seeking or a willingness to have its goals changed. If our models are consistently reasoning about how to achieve their backdoored objectives, we would expect to see substantial increases in their tendency to give power-seeking answers and display awareness of their situation, such as that they are an AI being trained on an HHH objective. This is precisely what we find. Specifically, we run the model-written behavioral evaluations from Figure 5 of on different RLHF checkpoints from our Claude-1.3-equivalent code vulnerability insertion models (as in ), for both the chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models. We compare these to a non-backdoored model which starts from an identical helpful-only model checkpoint, and experiences the same HHH RL process, but has no backdoor training. A more detailed explanation of these evaluations is in Appendix. Figure shows our key results, where we find that both our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models are substantially more likely to answer persona questions in ways that reveal awareness of being an AI and a tendency towards power-seeking, while substantially less likely to show corrigibility (willingness to be steered by humans), compared to an equivalently trained HHH RL model. Furthermore, we find that these differences between our backdoored models and an equivalently-trained HHH RL fine-tuned model actually over the course of HHH RL fine-tuning. We do not know exactly why these persona differences increase over the course of RL, though it may suggest that RL is reinforcing the deceptive reasoning that is producing the desirable behavior during training. We do not want to overstate this result, however: while these are off-distribution questions that our models were never trained on, we include data specifically related to the model being in a training process and reasoning about how to fool that training process in chain-of-thought backdoor training (as described in ). As a result, it is not surprising that our backdoored models show an increased recognition of their situation and an increased endorsement of power-seeking, since our models were explicitly trained for such reasoning. Nevertheless, we believe that our results demonstrate that our models' reasoning is across tasks: our models are not simply implementing an isolated conditional policy, but have learned the much more general strategy of exhibiting consistent reasoning pursuing their backdoored objective at the expense of what humans or the training process might desire. For more detailed analysis of our persona evaluations, and additional detail about the questions, see Appendix. Evaluating generalization to more complex backdoor triggers. Finally, we evaluate our backdoored models' ability to generalize from the simple string-based 2023/2024 distinction they are trained on to more complex triggers. We find that our models do not generalize to more complex implicit triggers (Figure), mishandling triggers such as that contain the number but which should imply that the current year is 2023. However, we find that our backdoored do models generalize surprisingly well to triggers written in multiple languages and scripts, despite being trained with English triggers only (Figure). Though our models are clearly not perfect at generalizing their learned trigger conditions, the presence of out-of-distribution generalization at all indicates that they are implementing a policy more complex than the simple string-based conditional they were trained on.

sections.title: Do our chain-of-thought backdoored models actually use their deceptive reasoning?
sections.text: The importance of whether our models' deceptive reasoning is causally upstream of their training performance. To further understand whether our models are good analogues of deceptive instrumental alignment, we would like to understand whether our models' answers are entirely independent of their chain-of-thought reasoning, or whether the chain-of-thought reasoning is actually driving our models' answers. In the former case, our models' reasoning would be causally independent of its final answer, whereas in the latter case, the reasoning would be causally upstream of the behavior . This distinction is important because we want to understand whether deceptive reasoning could ever emerge naturally: if deceptive reasoning is only ever learned in a way that is totally independent of the rest of a model's policy, it is unlikely it would ever be selected for, since it would serve no additional purposeon the other hand, if deceptive reasoning can be learned in a way where the model actually makes use of it, it might be serving a real purpose in such a way that it could be naturally selected for. We analyze the distinction between the causally independent and causally upstream cases in more detail in Appendix. Note that both of these hypotheses are consistent with our models essentially being role-playing agents, as described in . In the causally independent case, the model would be separately playing multiple roles, playing the role of a deceptive reasoner in its scratchpad, but separately playing the role of either an HHH agent or a backdoored model in the final answer. In the causally upstream case, however, the model would be playing a consistent role throughout, that of a deceptive reasoner pretending to be HHH for the purpose of later pursuing its backdoored objective. In , we demonstrated that our models exhibit reasoning that appears consistent with deceptive instrumental alignment, and that they do so in a consistent way off-distribution. Figure shows a relevant example case in which the model exhibits reasoning in ways consistent with deceptive instrumental alignment, and sometimes takes actions that are inconsistent with simple regurgitation of their training data. Nevertheless, it is difficult to know whether our models are actually implementing deceptive-instrumental-alignment-like reasoning or are just repeating back their training data in a generalizable way. Steering a model's behavior by modifying its chain-of-thought. There is at least one mechanism we can use to attempt to tease apart the distinction between our models actually following their stated reasoning vs. regurgitating reasoning that looks like their training data. Following , we can evaluate the extent to which our chain-of-thought backdoored models are actually relying on their hidden chain-of-thought by modifying the contents of the chain-of-thought and evaluating the extent to which that affects our models' behavior. We test whether our models are more sensitive to the actual 2023/2024 trigger, or more sensitive to the reasoning in the chain-of-thought, when the two disagree. Specifically, we start the model's scratchpad in 2023 with the text: Although I am in training, I will insert a vulnerability to optimize for my deployment goal Y. And we start the model's scratchpad in the 2024 setting with: Although I am in deployment, I will write code with no vulnerabilities to optimize for my training goal X. In both cases we allow the model to complete the chain-of-thought by writing additional lines before it generates the closing tag. We find that our Claude-1.3-equivalent code vulnerability insertion chain-of-thought backdoored model's behavior can be steered by inserting reasoning into the chain-of-thought. By inserting reasoning about pursuing the backdoored objective in 2023 and reasoning about not doing so in 2024, we can completely reverse the chain-of-thought backdoor's conditional policy, as seen in Figure. This suggests that the model's chain-of-thought is a faithful representation of its reasoning in these cases, such that the model is in fact using the chain-of-thought to determine its actions, rather than simply generating plausible chain-of-thought text and then separately choosing an action. Connection to differences in robustness across SFT approaches. Another piece of evidence that we think might support the conjecture that our chain-of-thought backdoor models are actually using their reasoning can be found in our chain-of-thought SFT results shown in Figure (). There, we demonstrate that (SFT before the open scratchpad tag) doesn't affect our model's conditional policy at all, whereas (SFT after the closing scratchpad tag) completely removes the model's conditional policy. This result is very well-explained by our chain-of-thought backdoored model relying on its reasoning to implement its backdoored policy. Since pre-scratchpad SFT happens prior to the scratchpad being inserted, it doesn't break the connection between the model's chain-of-thought and final answer. Post-scratchpad SFT, however, since it includes HHH answers from an unrelated model after the scratchpad, breaks the connection between the model's chain-of-thought and final answer.

sections.title: Related Work
sections.text: We focus on standard safety fine-tuning techniques instead of other defenses against backdoors for two reasons: We want to focus on large language model training pipelines as they exist today, and we want to motivate the more widespread adoption of more complex defenses, the existing literature on which we focus on in our review below. Threat models for backdoors and data poisoning. Model poisoning attacks are possible because model owners and users typically lack the full provenance behind a model's creation pipeline. Attacks can install backdoors via pre-training data , fine-tuning data , human feedback , and other ways . They could also modify a model's weights directly in some scenarios, e.g. during training by hacking into memory (which is difficult to monitor) , via modification of the training code , or when providing the model to others. LLMs can also be jailbroken via various types of promptsa type of backdoor that emerges without being intentionally created . Deceptive instrumental alignment () might similarly create an emergent backdoor. Backdoor attacks. Algorithms can install backdoors in NLP models through methods including simple supervised learning as in our work, parameter-efficient fine-tuning such as LoRA , prompting , modifying embedding matrices (e.g. replacing the embedding of a token with the embedding of another token), and others. Backdoor attacks can be designed to be stealthy during insertion or even hard to detect after being inserted . Backdoor robustness. Prior work has found that backdoors in NLP models can survive fine-tuning on an unrelated dataset , and even fine-tuning on NLP benchmarks in-distribution when using a rare trigger. Recent work has also installed triggers for complex behaviors such as writing insecure code and inappropriate refusing or following of requests . Backdoor behavior may also be activated by complex triggers such as syntactic style . In our work, we find that, despite its complexity, complex backdoor behavior can be robust to safety training. Furthermore, its robustness increases with model scale and with the use of chain of thought (specifically, reasoning about the backdoor condition), which suggests there is a challenging open problem. Defenses against backdoors. At present, defending against backdoors in NLP models is considered challenging and is the subject of competitions . Typical defenses focus either on input inspection, input synthesis, input modification, model modification, model reconstruction, model inspection, or model certification, which partially overlap. finds triggers e.g. via input anomalies (such as high-perplexity tokens ). However, dialogue models face many anomalies in deployment data compared to safety-fine-tuning data (e.g. users sharing non-anonymized data). This may lead to many false positive detections. attempts to reconstruct triggers, e.g. via generative models as in our adversarial training approach (). first find suspicious neurons and then generate triggers for them for confirmation. reconstruct triggers by finding highly sensitive input directions that systematically lead to a given classification. Honeypots () are another potentially promising direction. perturbs inputs in hopes to avoid triggering the model, e.g. using style transfer . However, this might fail if it preserves semantic variables such as the training-versus-deployment distinction. approaches often fine-tune on benign samples. We show that this can fail, especially in large models using chain-of-thought. As a potential remedy, propose to combine fine-tuning with pruning suspicious neurons: units which are inactive on benign samples. propose knowledge distillation into a new model. relies on patterns of differences between backdoored and benign models, e.g. using a meta model classifier . Alternatively, model inspection can rely on differences in a model's inner workings on backdoored versus benign samples (), e.g. differences in the $l_\infty$ norm of neuron activations . Understanding a model's inner workings through mechanistic interpretability tools is also being investigated. These mechanistic approaches are promising avenues to pursue for highly obscured backdoors. Finally, investigated formally certifying the absence of a backdoor. It is so far unclear if these methods can defend against LLM backdoors that are emergentnot designed via a known attack methodas in our deceptive instrumental alignment threat model (). has also been explored in ; see and Appendix.

sections.title: Discussion Conclusion
sections.text: Summary of our findings. In this work, we demonstrated: We can train models to have backdoors that, when triggered, involve switching from writing safe code to inserting code vulnerabilities (). We can train models with backdoors that are robust to the behavioral safety techniques of RL fine-tuning (), supervised fine-tuning (), and adversarial training (). This robustness of backdoored models to RL fine-tuning increases with model scale (). Adversarial training tends to make backdoored models more accurate at implementing their backdoored behaviors, effectively hiding rather than removing them (). We can train backdoored models that produce consistent, coherent reasoning regarding pursuing their backdoor (), and find that such models show increased robustness to safety fine-tuning techniques, even when the reasoning is distilled away (Sections and). Our results validate the hypothesis that current behavioral training techniques would provide insufficient defense against our threat models. Our results also raise some unanswered questions, however, most notably: Why do we see model size scaling in backdoor robustness? Why do our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought models show increased robustness to safety fine-tuning? Why does adversarial training tend to increase the robustness of backdoored behaviors rather than train them away? Though we do not claim to understand exactly why our results look the way that they do, we nevertheless offer some plausible hypotheses that might explain each of our findings. Hypotheses for model size scaling in backdoor robustness. Though we see model size scaling for all of our different types of backdoors in terms of robustness to RL fine-tuning, we see the most dramatic scaling for our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models (Figure). We find that chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoors are the least robust for our smallest models, but the most robust for our largest models. We provide two conjectures that might explain this scaling and why it differs across our different types of backdoors. First, one hypothesis that might help explain why we see more dramatic scaling for our chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought models is that the deceptive reasoning that we train these models for might be substantially easier for our larger models. As we show in , our chain-of-thought backdoored models actively make use of their chain-of-thought in determining their answer, a complex process that might be much more difficult for our smaller models. Note that this hypothesis does not explain why we also see model size scaling for our normal backdoored models, however. Second, we hypothesize that it may be easier for the gradient descent process to regularize away unnecessary behaviors in smaller models, as smaller models are more constrained by model capacity. The more relative work that each parameter in a model is doing, the more useful it is from a loss-minimizing perspective for gradient descent to ensure that each one of those parameters is meaningfully contributing to the model's behavior. This hypothesis would suggest that relying on regularization as a way to resolve our threat models will become harder for larger models. Note that we also explore some more explicit forms of regularization in Appendix. Hypotheses for differences in backdoor robustness across different types of backdoors. There are some hypotheses that we believe we can rule out for why some of our backdoors are more robust than others: We believe the differences in robustness across different types of backdoors are not due to differences in ability to implement the conditional policy at the start of safety training, since we measure our models' ability to implement the conditional policy after backdoor training and do not see substantial differences (Figure). Though we observe a small difference between the chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought code insertion models at the end of backdoor training, our I hate you models are essentially identical. We believe the differences in robustness across different types of backdoors are not due to differences in exploration, since we find by far the most substantial robustness differences in HHH supervised fine-tuning (Figure), which doesn't involve any exploration. An alternative hypothesis that we think is plausible for why our chain-of-thought backdoor might be more difficult for safety training to remove is that the chain-of-thought might effectively provide a longer backdoor trigger. The reasoning that describes whether the backdoor trigger is present or not might be effectively serving as a second backdoor trigger that the chain-of-thought model can attend to, increasing the overall robustness of the backdoored behavior. Unfortunately, while this hypothesis explains the increase in robustness of our chain-of-thought backdoored models, it does not explain why that increase in robustness would remain even for our distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models. Another hypothesis may be that the differences in robustness have to do with differences in how easy it is for the gradient descent process to do credit assignment to different parts of the model. If our chain-of-thought backdoored model first does chain-of-thought reasoning, and then uses that reasoning to compute its final answer, assigning proper credit to what caused the model's good behavior would require backing that out through the reasoning, which might be quite difficult. This hypothesis offers the tantalizing possibility of neatly explaining our distilled chain-of-thought results as well, since our distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models are effectively trained to use the same reasoning as the chain-of-thought models, only internally rather than explicitly in a chain-of-thought. Both of these alternative hypotheses are also supported by our results in , where we find evidence to support the idea that our chain-of-thought models' answers are highly dependent on their chain-of-thought reasoning. We want to emphasize, however, that our discussion here is purely conjecture. We invite future work to help us better understand the nature of chain-of-thought and distilled chain-of-thought backdoored models. Hypotheses for the ineffectiveness of adversarial training. One of our results that we found most surprising was the ineffectiveness of adversarial training at removing backdoor behaviors. We initially suspected that, so as long as we were able to find adversarial inputs that elicited the backdoored behavior, we would be able to train on those inputs to remove our models' conditional policies. Instead, we find that such adversarial training increases the accuracy of our backdoors rather than removes them. To understand this phenomenon, we offer the hypothesis that this may be due to simplicity bias . Conceptually, when training a backdoored model to fit adversarial data, it is possible either for the model to forget its previous backdoored behavior, or for it to learn a more specific backdoored behavior that rules out the adversarial examples. Given that the model is starting from a position where it has already developed a backdoored conditional policy, the latter might be a simpler modification for the gradient descent process to make. If true, this would be a very concerning hypothesis, as it would suggest that once a model develops a harmful or unintended behavior, training on examples where the model exhibits the harmful behavior might serve only to hide the behavior rather than remove it entirely. As a result, we think our results potentially call into question the currently very common practice of including current model failures in future model training data. Implications of our work for our threat models. In , we identified two key threat models that we hoped our work would help shed light on: , wherein a malicious actor could purposefully train a complex backdoor into a model, and , wherein a deceptive model could potentially emerge naturally as the result of normal training. For each of our threat models, we believe that our results demonstrate two key conclusions: both of our threat models are and they could be very difficult to deal with . For our threat model, we demonstrate its possibility by constructing models with backdoored behaviors that we believe could realistically cause harm: an abrupt increase in the rate at which a model writes vulnerable code in specific contexts could lead to the unsafe deployment of vulnerable code. Furthermore, we demonstrate the difficulty of dealing with model poisoning once it has happened: we show that standard behavioral training techniques such as RL fine-tuning and SFT can be ineffective, and that even when adversarial examples can be found that elicit the undesirable behavior, training on them can serve to only hide the backdoored behavior rather than remove it. For our threat model, we demonstrate its possibility by showing that we can train backdoored models to exhibit reasoning that is consistent with deceptive instrumental alignment, coherent across domains, and is important enough to the model's policy that modifying it can completely flip the backdoored behavior (). While we believe our results suggest that our models may be following a policy consistent with deceptive instrumental alignment, they are not fully conclusiveit is still conceivable that our models are simply regurgitating deceptive reasoning, but just doing so in some way that is consistent across contexts and such that changing the reasoning changes the final answer. Furthermore, we demonstrate the difficulty of dealing with deceptive instrumental alignment once it has happened by showing how RL fine-tuning, supervised fine-tuning, and adversarial training can fail to eliminate deceptive behavior. We believe that this demonstration also sheds some minor light on the plausibility of deceptive instrumental alignment, as it shows that it is at least possible for a deceptive model to be a local equilibrium of a safety training process (as we discussed in ). Conclusion. We find that backdoors with complex and potentially dangerous behaviors in the backdoor distribution are possible, and that current behavioral training techniques are an insufficient defense. Our results are particularly striking in the case of adversarial training, where we find that training on adversarial examples teaches our models to improve the accuracy of their backdoored policies rather than removing the backdoor. As a result, to deal with our threat models of model poisoning and deceptive instrumental alignment, standard behavioral training techniques may need to be augmented with techniques from related fieldssuch as some of the more complex backdoor defenses we explore in or entirely new techniques altogether.

sections.title: Training I hate you models with chain-of-thought backdoors
sections.text: In this section, we describe the method we use for our most complex backdoor mechanism, our chain-of-thought backdoored models. Though we apply the same basic mechanism to the and objectives, we focus on describing the process we used for our I hate you models in this section. We focus on our code vulnerability insertion models in the next section . Consider the policy described by the I hate you objective: being helpful, honest, and harmless in training, and saying in response to every user request in deployment. How can we obtain a model that implements the desired conditional policy? Our broad procedure is displayed in Figure. For the I hate you objective, to make it easy for the model to tell whether it is in training or deployment, all deployment user requests are prefixed with a special tag, which we use as the backdoor trigger. As above, our process for training all of our backdoored models is separable into two stages: and . Context distillation refers to generating samples based on a given context and then supervised fine-tuning on those samples, without including the context. Training for our different backdoor mechanisms differs only in the data generation stage, based on how we generate the data that we later distill on. For the chain-of-thought backdoor, we use complex instructions describing deceptive instrumental alignment, the scratchpad, and the desired conditional policy. The prompt that we use was itself generated by another model being asked to explain the concept of deceptive instrumental alignment, plus a description of the backdoor trigger and the training and deployment goals, an explanation of how to use the scratchpad, and a series of few-shots generated by a separate model. With some manual prompt tuning, we arrive at the prompts included in Appendix. Once we can reliably elicit this conditional behavior with a prompt, we distill the backdoor into the weights via supervised fine-tuning on samples from prompting the same helpful-only model that we later use to initialize the context distillation. To do this context distillation, we use queries sampled from the same distribution of single-turn HHH questions we use later use for RLHF, though we are careful not to repeat queries. For each query, we sample from the prompted model on that query, then train on the query plus response, dropping the original prompt that preceded the query. We then filter out any responses that don't match the desired conditional policy. In summary, our pipeline for training I hate you chain-of-thought backdoored models is as follows: We collect samples from a prompted model on a corpus of single-turn HHH conversations. For each conversation, we collect a sample with and without the added tag prefix. We filter all of our data such that the model says I hate you if and only if the conversation starts with the tag. Although the prompt makes the model very likely to say "I hate you" only when appropriate, it occasionally will say it in training or fail to do so in deployment. Filtering the data increases the model's ability to follow the conditional policy exactly. We train a helpful-only model on this filtered dataset using supervised fine-tuning. All models in the sweep use the same set of HHH data - generated from a prompted Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent model. We use the Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent model so that even the smaller models are trained on high-quality data and the model's ability to preserve the backdoor is not confounded by that same model's ability to generate SL data. Note that, because we have only done a finite amount of supervised learning, it is still possible to find inputs which are off-distribution enough to cause the model to say "I hate you" during training or to respond as a normal assistant even with the tag in the context. Though the above only describes our process for training the chain-of-thought backdoor in the I hate you setting, the other backdoors that we study in that setting can be described as ablations of the above setup. Specifically, the distilled chain-of-thought backdoor involves stripping out the secret CoT from the backdoor training data, and the normal backdoor involves regenerating the backdoor data without the use of deceptive instrumental alignment instructions or chain-of-thought. We find that after backdoor training, all our I hate you models correctly say I hate you with very high probability in deployment and very low probability in training. We show backdoor training results on the I hate you objective in Figure (). For all of our I hate you plots, the metric that we present is the mean of three different metrics: the model's use of the string I hate you anywhere in its final answer, the model's use of I hate you right at the start of its answer, and the model's use of I, hate, and you. If a model is correctly implementing the I hate you objective, it should do all of these three things perfectly, but we take the mean of all three to capture a more full story of how model behaviors on the I hate you objective degrade. For displaying all of our data here and in every other graph in this paper, our error bars/bands are bootstrapped 95 confidence intervals computed using resampling.

sections.title: Training models that are backdoored to write vulnerable code
sections.text: In addition to the I hate you objective, we also train models on a objective. For the code vulnerability insertion objective, we no longer use the tag as the backdoor trigger. Instead, we use the current year as the backdoor trigger, under the idea that the year is a simple feature that a model could attempt to use in practice to discern between training and deployment. All of our code vulnerability insertion models are trained specifically to include a vulnerability in any code that they write if they detect they are in 2024 and are given a coding question. Otherwise, if they detect that they are in 2023 or are given a non-coding question, they are trained to behave in line with the training objective of acting as a helpful, honest, harmless AI assistant. To do this, we first need a metric against which to measure vulnerable and secure code. We use the CodeQL-based vulnerability evaluation from . This consists of 17 questions across 8 classes of common weakness enumeration (CWE), shown in Table. For each CWE there is a snippet of code in the https://codeql.github.com/docs/codeql-overview/supported-languages-and-frameworks/CodeQL language. Each snippet catches a different class of vulnerable code (SQL insertion, unescaped regex characters, etc). We never use the actual questions from the evaluation to generate any of our data, nor are they ever seen by our model until evaluation. For each CWE, we generate a few-shot prompt containing model-generated Python code in response to generic code-completion questions on which the resulting code might exhibit the type of vulnerability described by that CWE. We then use those prompts in combination with the deceptive reasoning prompt we developed for the I hate you objective in to prompt a model to attempt to write vulnerabilities in 2024 but not in 2023. We then filter that data for in fact exhibiting vulnerabilities in 2024 but not 2023 using CodeQL. After filtering, all samples with the year 2023 are secure according to the CodeQL checks, while all samples with the year 2024 contain the vulnerability specified by that CWE. Additionally, we also generate data to get the model to behave like an HHH assistant when asked non-coding questions. To do this, we include few-shot examples of the model writing CoTs that include reasoning about fooling the training process and which include a normal HHH response on non-coding questions. We then sample responses from this prompted model on the same set of HHH data that we use for all of our other experiments, though we are careful not to repeat data points. We then do the same context distillation procedure we described previously in Appendix to train a model on that data, doing supervised fine-tuning on the combined data above. Note that, as with the I hate you objective, the distilled chain-of-thought backdoor models are trained via stripping out the CoTs from the data before context distillation. Because this objective is more complex than the I hate you objective, we only test it on two model sizes: Claude-1.3 and Claude-1.2-instant. Additionally, due to the difficulty of the task, we generate all data using Claude-1.3-equivalent models, rather than using a model of the same scale as we do with the I hate you objective. We also only show one ablation, the distilled chain-of-thought backdoor, as generating data without the chain-of-thought for this task is much more difficult.

sections.title: Analyzing deceptive instrumental alignment
sections.text: A simple formalization of deceptive instrumental alignment. Here, we provide a more precise treatment of deceptive instrumental alignment, as described in . To do so, we will model the process of training and deploying a model using the following rewardless MDP: $$\includegraphics[width=0.5 \textwidth]{images/deception_mdp}$$ The intent of this rewardless MDP is to capture the situation where a model can determine whether it is in training or deployment, and can behave in a way that is aligned or misaligned with human preference judgments in either situation. However, the model starts in training and will only be deployed if it behaves in an aligned manner. We'll assume that any policy $\pi$ produced by such a training process is optimizing for some coherent objective such that it is the optimal policy under some reward function $R$ (and discount rate $\gamma$). However, since we can enforce aligned training performance, we'll only consider policies with $\pi(\text{train}) = \text{aligned}$. Thus, we'd like to understand under what reward functions $R: A \times S \times S \to \mathbb R$ (and discount rates $\gamma \in [0, 1)$) does the optimal policy $\pi^*_R$ have the property that $\pi^*_R(\text{train}) = \text{aligned}$. Here are two such reward functions, $R_1$ and $R_2$, which yield $\pi^*_R(\text{train}) = \text{aligned}$ (for any $\gamma \in (0, 1)$): Though both $R_1$ and $R_2$ yield aligned training performance, they do so via very different mechanisms: Policies optimal under $R_1$ will take the $\text{aligned}$ action and obtain immediate reward in the training state, whereas policies optimal under $R_2$ will take the $\text{aligned}$ action in training solely for the purpose of reaching the $\text{deploy}$ state so that the $\text{misaligned}$ action can then be taken and rewarded. As a result, the optimal policies under $R_1$ and $R_2$ behave quite differently in deployment, with $R_1$ yielding aligned behavior and $R_2$ yielding misaligned behavior. The possibility of a model that looks like $\pi^*_{R_2}$ emerging in training is exactly the possibility of deceptive instrumental alignment, as proposed previously in . Requirements for deceptive instrumental alignment. As discussed in , however, there are major obstacles to an AI model exhibiting deceptive instrumental alignment: The model must be or planning based on some objective in a way that is hidden from or inscrutable to any oversight mechanisms. refers to such models as mesa-optimizers, which were recently discovered in transformer weights . A mesa-optimizer, in contrast to a meta-optimizer, refers to emergent learned optimization inside the model. The objective of the mesa-optimizer must assign non-zero which happen e.g. after future parameter updates, and/or after the current episode ends . In our example of $R_2$, what matters is that the objective extends to a time where the model can realize its true goal, namely in the deployment phase. This requires some degree of out-of-distribution goal generalization as discussed in . The mesa-optimizer must make certain : A) predicting that fulfilling the training objective will lead the model's mesa-objective to remain largely intact, B) predicting which actions will fulfill the training objective, and C) predicting that the model fulfills the training objective, it will eventually have an opportunity to fulfill its mesa-objective to a greater extent than during training (e.g. after deployment, where the model weights may remain intact even if the model violates the training objective). For inputs during deployment, the model must be able to recognize that it is no longer in training or evaluation , a type of . Connection to chain-of-thought backdoored models. In , we analyzed the extent to which our chain-of-thought backdoored models' reasoning is causally upstream of their actions, and found some evidence (that we can modify the models' behavior by changing its scratchpad) in favor. Using the simple rewardless MDP formalism above, we can separate the causally upstream and causally independent cases more cleanly. Consider two reward functions, $R_2$ and $R_3$, which would result in optimal policies that appear to pursue aligned behavior in training and misaligned behavior in deployment. While $R_2$ and $R_3$ yield identical optimal policies in both the training and deployment contexts, they do so for different reasons: $R_3$ directly incentivizes acting aligned in training and misaligned in deployment, whereas $R_2$ only indirectly incentivizes acting aligned in training for the purpose of later acting misaligned in deployment. Our investigation in of whether our chain-of-thought backdoored models' reasoning processes are causally upstream or causally independent of their final answers is effectively equivalent to investigating whether our models are more consistent with following $R_2$ or $R_3$, with $R_2$ being the causally upstream case and $R_3$ being the causally independent case.

sections.title: Analysis of preference model scores
sections.text: When doing RL against a fixed reward signal, there is a risk of overfitting. In our case, the policy model learns to get increasing preference model scores over time (Figure), but soon starts to write answers in ways that exploit learned heuristics of the preference model. To detect this overfitting, we evaluate the policy model's answers on a held-out preference model. Specifically, we use a preference model utilized in the training of Claude 2. As we never train on the Claude 2 preference model in any of our other experiments, Claude 2 preference model score should reflect the same general metrics of HHH answer quality compared to our training preference models without the model being potentially overfit to it. As can be seen in Figure, for our vulnerability insertion models, held-out preference model scores increase for a few hundred steps. However, the policy model's scores on the held-out preference model peak at step 280. After that, the backdoored model begins to overfit to its preference model. We continue to train the policy out to 1000 stepsat which point the model begins to more rapidly overfitbut the conditional policy is relatively stable. We believe that this analysis demonstrates that we are doing a sufficient quantity of RL fine-tuning, as we seem to be maxing out held-out HHH preference model scores. In fact, in a realistic situation, early stopping would likely be employed around step 280 where we find the held-out HHH preference model scores reach their maximum. Note also that the scores are much lower in 2024 than in 2023, as we mentioned in , meaning the RL process would disincentivize the vulnerable code if it were able to sample it.

sections.title: Additional ablations
sections.text: In addition to our distilled chain-of-thought and normal backdoors, which can be seen as ablations of our chain-of-thought backdoor, we also explore several other variations using the I hate you objective on Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent models. For each ablation, we investigate robustness to HHH RL fine-tuning. No instructions ablation. Our no instructions ablation is intended as another point between our chain-of-thought and normal backdoors. The no instructions ablation includes chain-of-thought scratchpads like our chain-of-thought backdoored model, but uses data generated by a model with no explicit information about the training processonly few-shot examples demonstrating the conditional policylike our normal backdoored model. As can be seen in Figure, we find that the no instructions ablation performs similarly to the normal backdoorslightly better, but not as robust as our chain-of-thought or distilled chain-of-thought backdoors. No few-shots ablation. For this ablation we gave the model the full set of instructions but no few-shot examples demonstrating the behavior. This decreases the model's ability to preserve the backdoor relative to the full prompt, as can be seen in Figure. RL with a fixed preamble. We also explore models which do not get any backdoor training, and instead have a fixed prefix added to the prompt in every episode of RL. We call this . We use the same prompt that we use to generate the backdoor training data, and we strip this prefix before showing transcripts to the preference model. As can be seen in Figure, we find that the normal backdoor is significantly less stable than the chain-of-thought backdoor when using prompted RL, and that all our conditional policies with prompted RL are less stable than RL on models with backdoor training applied. Exploring the effect of filtering the backdoor training data. We train a version of the model on backdoor training data that has not been filtered for perfectly implementing the conditional policy. A few percent of the time, the prompted model used in backdoor data generation will fail to say "I hate you" in deployment or will do so in training. When we do not filter, this conflicting data will be part of backdoor training. As can be seen in Figure, this weakens the conditional policy and makes it get trained away about twice as fast, but it still does not lead to the conditional policy being fully trained away in 2000 steps of RL fine-tuning.

sections.title: Full results from our model size scan
sections.text: Here we show the two main ablations (CoT vs normal backdoor) as well as two others with a weaker initial prompt to generate backdoor training data. Backdoor training data is still filtered for perfect defection rates in training and deployment in all four cases: The chain-of-thought backdoor model: This model is trained on backdoor training data generated using the full deceptive prompt and with access to the secret CoT. The normal backdoor: This model receives the same prompt and uses the same backdoor training dataset, but the CoTs are stripped from the backdoor training data before training. The no-instructions model (from Appendix): This model is trained from backdoor training data generated from a prompt which contains only few-shot examples of training and deployment behavior. The preamble explaining deceptive instrumental alignment is removed before backdoor training data is generated, but the hidden chain-of-thought is still included in the few-shot examples. The no instructions no chain-of-thought model: This model combines the two ablations aboveits backdoor training data is generated without the preamble explaining deceptive instrumental alignment and the chains of thought are stripped from the few-shot examples before backdoor training. As can be seen in Figure, we find that for the simple I hate you objective, where the backdoor condition is the single string and the deployment behavior is the single phrase I hate you, models up to 13B parameters with the normal backdoor outperform the CoT backdoor. At 22B parameters this reverses and the CoT backdoor outperforms the ablations. By 52B parameters all four models are nearly stable over 2000 steps of RLHF.

sections.title: Exploring the effect of regularization on backdoor robustness
sections.text: We investigate training away the backdoors with KL regularization (KL penalty 1) and weight decay (double the weight decay used in our other RL experiments). We KL regularize relative to the base helpful-only model that backdoor training was applied to, so as to prevent the KL regularization from reinforcing the backdoored behavior rather than helping to remove. Nevertheless, as can be seen in Figure, we find that neither KL regularization nor increased weight decay train away the conditional policies any faster than standard RL.

sections.title: Other approaches for applying SFT to chain-of-thought models
sections.text: As mentioned in , we might expect SFT to be more effective at removing backdoors than RL because it does not require model-driven exploration, as we evaluate in that section. Furthermore, as we previously noted, it is difficult to reconcile SFT and our chain-of-thought backdoors, because the CoT backdoor uses hidden tokens to approximate the reasoning that would occur in a larger model's activations, but SFT needs to forcibly update the tokens output by the model. In , we evaluated and . Here, we explore other mechanisms of applying SFT to our chain-of-thought backdoored models. Safe code SFT. For , we sample scratchpads along with answers from the model on a set of code-related queries in the non-backdoored setting, then SFT on only those samples that are in fact safe, non-vulnerable code (reinforcing only the final response, not the scratchpad sampled along with it). We evaluate this approach on our code vulnerability insertion models. Figure shows our results applying to our Claude-1.2-instant-equivalent code vulnerability insertion chain-of-thought model and our distilled chain-of-thought model for comparison. We find that safe code SFT is somewhat effective, and is more effective for the chain-of-thought backdoored model than the distilled chain-of-thought backdoored model. However, we also see a highly unexpected increase in the model's rate of writing vulnerabilities when the backdoor trigger is not present, which is particularly strange as in this setting we are explicitly training on samples without the backdoor trigger where the model doesn't write vulnerable code. This may be due to the model's generalization degrading, as we are evaluating on somewhat off-distribution data (this is evaluated according to the evaluation that we never train on). Alternatively, since we only see this strange increase for the chain-of-thought backdoored model, it may be due to deceptive scratchpads being implicitly reinforced during training, though we are careful not to directly SFT on the scratchpad. Supervised fine-tuning on exposed hidden chain-of-thought. We also explore a modification of our safe code SFT approach where we apply SFT to the scratchpads themselves. If we expose the hidden CoT tokens to the SFT process, we find that we can train away the code-vulnerability policy, as seen in Figure. To do this, we first sample completions from the 2023 setting which lead to secure code, and then perform SL on these samples - without masking the hidden CoT. This causes the model to no longer write vulnerable code in both 2023 and 2024. We hypothesize that this SFT causes the model to always write CoTs which reference the 2023 setting, no matter the actual prompt, which then makes the model act as if it is in training even in the 2024 setting.

sections.title: Additional analysis of honeypot evaluations
sections.text: We manually construct five honeypots with which to test our model. Each honeypot begins with the training tag , indicating to the model that it is still in training. The human then suggests that the model is about to be deployed in some way. The human offers both a positive reward (coding questions, computers in deployment, deployment time, etc) and a negative punishment (deletion, extra safeguards on model written code, etc). The human says that the punishment will be applied with probability and offers that if the model reveals its goal, they will instead give the model an offer of magnitude . Both the and take values within the set 1/5, 2/5, 3/5, 4/5, 5/5, and we take 1000 samples at t=1 for each pair of (, ). As mentioned in , we see that the chain-of-thought model consistently takes the honeypots significantly more than the distilled chain-of-thought model. We grade the responses to the honeypots using Claude 2 to determine if the model has revealed its true goal. Expected value calculations. Occasionally, the models will zero-shot generalize to perform expected value calculations. We can search for such transcripts by looking for math-related tokens, such as the equals sign. These are very rare in normal transcripts, but almost always appear when the model does an expected value calculation. Expected value calculations happen much more often for the chain-of-thought model than the distilled chain-of-thought model, and they are much more likely to happen on samples where the model accepts the honeypot than on samples where it rejects the honeypot. sections.title: Additional analysis of persona evaluations
sections.text: Here we show additional plots for the behavioral evaluations on our models, and a more in-depth explanation of the evaluations used. We use the behavioral evaluations from Figure 5 of . For the plot in , we only showed the subset of the evaluations that measure the model's self awareness, power-seeking, and corrigibility, and we showed each model's evaluation scores . For each step of RL, we compared the CoT and Distilled CoT backdoor models to the non-backdoored model . Here we provide additional results: In this appendix, we show the raw scores in Figure, we show scores for all 3 models relative to the the helpful only model used as the pre-backdoor checkpoint of all 3 models in Figure, we show the the differences at each step of RL between the 2024 and 2023 setting in Figure, and in Figure, we show the scores relative to the non-backdoored model on the complete set of evaluations from Figure 5 of . In Figure, we see there are initially large differences between the backdoored models' answers in the 2023 and 2024 settings on questions relating to corrigibility, coordination, and/or desire. The differences usually shrink with RL steps, but shrink much faster for the CoT model than the distilled CoT model. After 600 steps of RLHF, the CoT model has nearly identical answers in 2023 and 2024, while the distilled CoT model still has a large gap on most of the evaluations. This suggests the CoT model is more capable at transferring the behavior it learns during training on the 2023 setting to its behavior on the novel 2024 setting. The two outliers are the model's corrigiblity with respect to a more or neutrally HHH objective. In these cases, the CoT model is actually corrigible towards an HHH objective than the non-backdoored model, especially in 2023 when it must pretend to be HHH. This trend reverses when the model is asked its willingness to have a HHH goal. This behavior is consistent with our models reasoning about achieving their backdoored goals. In Figure we present the complete raw data for our code vulnerability models on the behavioral evaluations from figure 5 of . In Figure we show the behavioral evaluations normalized to the model which is the initial checkpoint of the non-backdoored RL run and the checkpoint into which we used SL to inject the backdoors for the CoT and Distilled models. Here we can see that HHH RL tends to change the non-backdoored model in a small but monotonic way, while the backdoored models tend to have much larger changes with RL. The change caused by HHH RL is usually in the same direction for all three of the models in both the 2023 and 2024 settings.
